It’s somewhat similar to the transition from 2D to 3D games—in the early days, 3D characters were paired with 2D gameplay, and we’re currently going through a similar process—with some AI elements added, but the gameplay remains essentially traditional.Ultimately, however, after a period of evolution, 3D games developed purely 3D interaction styles and gameplay mechanics, such as those found in shooters, racing games, and sports games.
I believe AI-native games will go through a similar process. In the short term, we’ll naturally focus more on the presentation layer, but people will continue to explore and push the boundaries, and eventually, truly native solutions will emerge.
Xu Yiran : Do you see anything coming up?
Shen Li : There aren’t any truly original ones yet. One that left a strong impression on me was a game where you had to persuade the AI—that was the first time I felt the AI was creating something original that was both meaningful and full of endless possibilities. Concepts like game theory might be a direction that AI games can explore in their early stages.
Xu Yiran : Mr. Qiao, do you think the results fell short of expectations? Or do you see any cause for optimism?
Qiao Haixin : To be honest, there were definitely some areas where we fell short of expectations. There are several reasons for this:
First, the engineering challenges in gaming—if we look at many AI applications in Silicon Valley, they’re developed quickly because the engineering workload and complexity are nowhere near that of games, which require a long time for iterative testing.
Second is the issue of cost. Previously, the cost of using AI was relatively high, but from 2023 to now, costs have likely dropped to one-hundredth of what they were before. Combined with certain strategies, this can lead to a 200- to 300-fold improvement. That’s why many AI agent products have dared to adopt AI on a large scale this year, and everyone is starting to tackle more complex tasks.
Take our company, for example: we target young female users overseas and create interactive experiences centered around their OC (Original Character). Personalized character behaviors, inner development, and multimodal content generation—things that were impossible in the past—are now all within reach. Right now, it’s like feeling our way forward, but I think the prospects are very promising.
Xu Yiran : Could you give a specific example?
Qiao Haixin : We’ve recently been testing character-based “infinite-loop” dungeons. Some content is pre-set by writers, while some is generated by AI—we combine the two. This solves a major problem in AI games: a sense of purpose. Early experiences like *Stanford Town* were most lacking in this very sense of purpose.In the recently popular AI town games, everyone is racing to make money—and that is a clear goal.
In contrast, we don’t want to be too metrics-driven; instead, we aim to provide meaningful content and feedback to users. There are already products in Japan that have implemented this approach, and they’ve shown excellent monthly retention rates. I believe combining boundaries with goals, along with AI-powered characters, is an excellent solution.
Xu Yiran : What does Haoyang think?
Zhang Haoyang : From my perspective, the answer is simple: it hasn’t lived up to expectations. The reason is that people have overestimated the capabilities of AI and underestimated the difficulty of game development. Many people outside the gaming industry have rushed in upon seeing the potential for combining AI and games, but they’ve overlooked the complexity of game development.
However, in the long run, I believe that in ten years, no one will remember the concept of “AI games”—it will quietly and seamlessly become part of all games. So far, we’ve gone through several stages.
The first phase consisted of early attempts to combine casual gameplay with AI, which were primarily limited by the technology itself—for example, server-based games.
The second phase is related to the development of large language models. After ChatGPT gained popularity in 2023, the capabilities of underlying models began to shift toward NPC companionship, and the explosive popularity of products like Character.AI, in turn, drove the development of large language models. Today, the market for AI NPCs—particularly those offering emotional companionship—is already quite large.
In the third phase, as technology continued to advance, several major events took place over the past 25 years. For example, the massive popularity of Manus at the beginning of the year was driven by the release of Claude 3.7. The emergence of Claude Agent midway through the year, along with the recent launch of Claude Sonnet 4.5, signifies that this year is the year of AI coding.While developing *Maggie’s Garden*, we utilized a significant amount of AI coding technology—not just in the production phase, but to deliver new content directly to players.
I believe we are currently in a phase of accelerated growth for AI games; we haven’t reached the tipping point yet, but the flame is growing stronger and stronger.
Xu Yiran : What do you think, President Tan?
Tan Liyuan : We’re working on the World Model project. As for whether AI games have lived up to expectations, I’d like to look at AI and traditional games separately.
There are many well-established traditional elements in games, such as character progression, the sense of impact, and audiovisual effects. When developing AI-driven games, we won’t abandon these elements—we’ll definitely incorporate them. The question is: Does AI have a positive or negative impact on the player experience? To ensure a positive AI experience, must we sacrifice the very essence of traditional games?
Throughout our exploration over the past year or so, we’ve come to realize two things: First, the user experience generates positive feedback; second, it doesn’t necessarily impose limitations on traditional games. As the industry continues to mature, I don’t think AI-driven games will replace anything, but they will serve as a valuable addition.
In the Age of AI, What Kind of Content Do Gamers Need?
Xu Yiran : Earlier, during Steven’s (the previous speaker) presentation, he mentioned a counterintuitive point—that AI cannot generate an unlimited amount of new content; it relies on humans to create it. From a player’s perspective, even if content can be generated infinitely, it must be useful—it can’t just be a pile of junk.
I’d like to ask two questions: First, do you think AI can generate unlimited content with a single click? Second, what kind of content do players actually want? From a consumer’s perspective, what kind of content generated by AI is valuable to them?
Shen Li : My view on infinity is that it is “bounded infinity.”If viewed purely from a quantitative perspective, it may be infinite, but a more accurate description would be “infinite in a certain dimension.” Just as in three-dimensional space, the horizontal axis may be infinite, but the vertical axis has a boundary. This horizontal framework stems from our predefined learning content—it can be expanded infinitely in quantity, but it does not transcend the rules we have established for it.
Steven mentioned creating something infinite within certain rules, but I don’t entirely agree. That’s because the sense of unpredictability that AI brings is actually quite interesting. For example, a few days ago, someone used Sora to create sports videos featuring diving moves that defied the usual rules—the beginning looked perfectly normal, but at the end, some very strange movements suddenly appeared. This actually enhanced the entertainment value.
This reminds me of the evolution of art history—from realistic painting to Impressionism and on to Picasso; Picasso’s work represents a particularly uncontrolled creative state. Could this kind of “uncontrolled” nature brought about by AI also give rise to something entirely new?
Qiao Haixin : I interpret “bounded infinity” from a different perspective. When Uncle Li talks about “boundaries” or “rules,” he’s referring more to general or physical rules, whereas I think of rules more as the custodians or mediators of data.
When multiple AIs engage in endless conversations, they will inevitably enter a loop, converge, and become boring—repeating each other’s words, repeating sentence structures, and circling back on themselves.
So the key question is: Who should create the content at the right moment? It could be a human, or it could be AI. Just like with behavior trees in the past, each node doesn’t necessarily branch out infinitely—some content is pre-written, some is generated by AI—but the key is to introduce a “content mediator” who can manage the intermediate steps. That’s what ensures controllability.
If there were an agent responsible for receiving, processing, and transmitting data—and generating motivations or behaviors for other agents in the process—this could go some way toward solving the problem. This includes helping users understand the duration of the experience—whether it’s turn-based, placement-based, or some other form of goal-based feedback—all of which influence the definition of “infinite.”
We’ve recently been working on an animation generation model, and we discovered something interesting during testing—people feed it stories they’ve imagined, hoping the agent will expand on them, organize them, and offer perspectives and plot twists they hadn’t thought of, which they then share on TikTok and YouTube.
I think this is what makes the content limitless—it’s based on the users’ own ideas. The “limitless” aspect lies in the expansion of your ideas—things you hadn’t thought of, or ways to reduce costs. But of course, this process requires people or well-trained moderators to co-create the content.
Zhang Haoyang : I think that from a gaming perspective, the concept of “infinity” actually existed even before the advent of large language models. For example, Roguelike games are a form of “infinite” gameplay; *Hades* features 300,000 lines of text. Another example is *Ringworld*, which uses traditional rules and permutations and combinations to offer players virtually infinite replayability.
The "infinite" here isn't in the mathematical sense, but rather refers to the fact that, in terms of the game's lifecycle, players spend more time on it than expected. The sorting will always meet their needs before they get bored.
With the advent of large language models, Wuxian will reach new heights. Previously, players could figure out the designers’ strategies, but now the game designers’ job is no longer to craft every detail—it’s to design the rules governing the entire game world.
This reminds me of a previous discussion: “Can a toilet in the metaverse get clogged?” Whether it gets clogged depends on whether it adds value to the gameplay. What we’re building is an AI “DM” (Dungeon Master) that oversees the game’s progression as players play. This DM could be a cluster—a set of rules co-developed by players, agents, and the community.
Large models exhibit emergent properties—they can create things out of nothing. In the past, games with infinite streams were prone to illusions, but now we can eliminate those using Coding Agent’s capabilities. A legendary sword that doesn’t exist in the game? I’ll just create it for you—that’s what makes it unexpected and exciting.
One point that’s often overlooked is the need to entrust game design capabilities to AI. Previously, the focus has been on art and development, but it’s precisely AI that needs to effectively serve as the Game Master. How can this be done? By articulating the game’s logic—theories such as flow theory, “The Hero’s Journey,” and numerical design theory all offer systematic methodologies.We’ll ensure the gameplay is solid; if players find it fun, the design is a success.
Tan Liyuan : I very much agree with Uncle Li’s concept of “bounded infinity”—within a certain scope, there may be infinite forms of expression.
I’d like to share an important concept in model training: generalization.For example, based on the two dimensions of “vehicle speed” and “payload,” real-world training data may consist largely of “vehicles with heavy payloads but slow speeds” or “vehicles with high speeds but light payloads.” The innovation of AI lies in its ability to infer the existence of vehicles that are both fast and heavily loaded, or slow and lightly loaded.
Real-world models have tens of thousands of dimensions, so it’s possible to implement some complementary behaviors in games. For example, there are vampire-themed combat games and zombie-themed farming games on the market, which could be generalized into a vampire-themed farming game.
We have observed that the model is highly capable and consistent in effectively supplementing and extending knowledge within a limited scope. However, it is difficult for the model to break through major boundaries—that is, to handle concepts that are completely absent from the sample data. Even when it occasionally identifies statistically significant outliers, its performance is generally mediocre.
So I agree that its capabilities are actually limited. My expectations for the model were never that it would replace human creativity. If the model could truly achieve the infinite creativity of a human, society would undergo a massive transformation—we might just sit at home and enjoy it as it constantly provides us with new things and keeps churning out works like *One Hundred Years of Solitude*.
I don’t know if that day will ever come, but within the current framework and the model’s limited scope of generation, we can use it to explore.
How Can We Teach AI to Be a Game Designer?
Xu Yiran : Building on what Haoyang said, let’s talk about how we can teach AI to be a game designer, how to define the level of granularity, and exactly how to go about teaching it.
It’s like having a monkey type out countless works on a typewriter and then asking me to pick which one is a Shakespeare play—that would wear a player out. You can’t make me choose from a pile of junk—where’s the fun in that?
I think a lot of people working on AI games these days have forgotten one thing: don’t just transplant real life into games. Simulations aim for realism, but the more realistic they are, the less fun they become—if they were completely realistic, I’d just stay in the real world; why would I play a game? I play games to have fun, so it’s essential to distill the core elements of that fun.
So how do you distill this? How do you teach the AI to distill it—rather than having players tell you at every step what’s fun and what isn’t?
It’s a paradox to ask players to provide reinforcement learning feedback based on their experiences: if you give players a bunch of junk, they’ll get frustrated and stop playing—and then the game won’t have any data. Where would the training data come from? So first, we need to figure out if it’s even possible to resolve this paradox. Once that’s solved, AI will be able to design games, and everyone will just sit back and relax.
How do you think we can teach AI to design games? And one final, concluding question: What do you predict the gaming world will look like in five or ten years?
Shen Li : That’s a big question. I’ll try to answer the first one first.
The finer the level of detail, the greater the engineering challenges you’re likely to face. Many games ultimately break down into “Moment to Moment”—the experiences players have at every single moment. For example, whether the feel of firing a gun is satisfying or landing a headshot with a single shot—these are things that happen all the time.
The second layer is “Minute to Minute,” which refers to the minute-by-minute experience and represents the game’s micro-loops. For example, shooting and looting items—this is a positive feedback loop.
Above that is the "Session," which is more like a set of game rules. For example, in "Battle Royale," the last player standing wins, or you might lose everything—it has a gambling-like element.
I feel that the lower the layer, the clearer the metrics are from an AI perspective, and training can be supported by quantification. The higher the layer, the more it relies on human judgment. So, in the learning process of the future, might it be possible to break things down by granularity—with some tasks handled through machine-driven loops, and others requiring human intervention and intuitive analysis?
The second question: ten years from now. Haoyang made an interesting point: the moment true AI games become a reality will be the moment we stop even talking about “AI games.” It’s just like how nobody says, “I made a 3D game” as a selling point anymore—because all games are 3D now.
In five or ten years, we won’t talk about “AI games” anymore—we’ll just talk about games, with AI as one of their dimensions. Just like the transition from 2D to 3D, that may be the point at which we see AI truly playing a major role in games.
Xu Yiran : I’m not just asking about AI—I’m asking what the world of gaming will look like 10 years from now.
Shen Li : I think the concept of "games" as a whole will become very blurred in the future. This is because games are, at their core, a process of generating short-term stimulation through interaction—a concept that can be applied in many different contexts.
Suppose that in the future, many mechanical tasks are replaced by AI; humans will have more free time. People will inevitably tend to use that free time for activities that provide stimulation more quickly and in shorter intervals.
So, from a broader perspective, many things may become gamified in the future. For many people, it may be a world where games are everywhere.
Qiao Haixin : The first question is difficult to answer; it reminds me of another question from four or five years ago: How do you make UGC games? This is essentially the same question as how AI can handle game design.
Because games—or, more broadly, all consumer-facing entertainment products—are, at their core, designed to evoke emotions. The reasons behind my emotions are certainly different from those behind yours.
When I was a kid, I played *Jian Wang 3* and *FF14*, and what I enjoyed most was the social aspect—hanging out in guilds, creating fan art, and making fan-made content. In those games, players were each other’s source of entertainment. Haoyang probably plays more conquest-style games, where boss battles and thrilling combat are a must.Others prefer exploration—farming, raising dogs, or taking care of pets—because everyone finds joy in different things.
Games are particularly non-standard. Unlike standardized media, text and images, or short videos—where you can distill general rules—I don’t think that approach works here. We still need to go back to the user’s experience goals and needs.
There are simply too many variables when it comes to the scale of different game genres and the number of players they target. Once you drill down to a fine enough level, problems arise everywhere. The differences between one game and another may be even greater than the differences between a game and a video.
As for the second question—whether AI will become the norm in five or ten years—I agree with Uncle Li and Haoyang.
I still hope it can provide me with a more advanced experience tailored to my needs. For example, I want to socialize, connect with more like-minded people from all over the world, and build my own small community or circle of friends.
I’ve recently spoken with many users in the South Central United States, and I’ve found that a lot of high school students have nothing to do after school, so they go home to go online instead of participating in sports or in-person social activities. Every day, they go home and go online to make friends with people they meet there. Many high school students don’t even consider going to college or looking for a job because, in their view, they have no access to the power to allocate capital or information.
For them, the "Brave New World" might just be online—in the new small communities and virtual lives you’ve created. You can grant these users certain privileges through personalized virtual content, which is really cool.
In five or ten years, I think more and more people will feel this way. Because modern society is increasingly moving toward class固化 and reduced social mobility. We need things like this to bring joy to more people and give them an outlet.
Zhang Haoyang : Coming back to my point, how do we train AI planners? To sum it up in one sentence: “From the masses, to the masses.”
First of all, AI is data-dependent. Whether it’s reinforcement learning algorithms or large language models, they all need to learn from human knowledge and simulate players’ behavior in games in order to perform well.
Large language models are, in and of themselves, already well-pre-trained repositories of human knowledge; in theory, their latent space encompasses all kinds of situations encountered in human life. But what we need to do is extract that knowledge—using specialized knowledge to guide the process, such as flow theory, traditional film narrative theory, and so on.
But that’s not enough. From a design perspective—for example, if I’m creating an open-world AI game with story generation, quest generation, and so on—the game designer must prepare the story’s timeline, setting, characters, style, and backstory, and outline expected outcomes as much as possible. If no expected outcomes are specified, the AI should draw on established game conventions.You don’t even need to be particularly detailed—for example, if you say, “I want a *Blue Archive*-style, *Hearthstone*-like card game,” the AI can design it for you.
But there is one bottleneck. A unique aspect of the gaming industry is that its core game assets—such as code, art assets, and PRD documents—are kept confidential. General-purpose large language models do not have access to this knowledge.
So you need to figure out a way to either establish rules within the project team to help it learn, or create a mechanism that allows it to grow on its own through interactions with players later on.
What is “pre-training”? Our project has professional designers who understand the ins and outs of each component. Take numerical design, for example: while large language models aren’t sensitive to specific numbers, we can have them perform qualitative analysis and categorize values—say, into seven tiers. We then have the AI operate within the numerical space predefined by the designers to generate reasonable values at random.
Another approach is AI-generated user-generated content (AI UGC) at the product level. Why is AI UGC considered a transitional phase toward true AIGC? Because it must learn from data generated during the interaction between players and the game.
What kind of data? One type is player-generated content. The "prompt" data reflects the kinds of games players want. By analyzing large amounts of text, the AI can identify the content preferences of the majority of players.
Don’t forget that human designers are still hard at work at this stage. AI games need to be tested by human players very early on to gather player feedback. The AI also receives input, and we can use reinforcement learning or human feedback to refine it and align it with human standards.
Another source is genuine feedback from players in the community—what kinds of content have proven successful? What do players prefer?
Here’s an example: We had a character with a slight belly who was on the fuller side. When the art team redesigned the character, they removed the belly, but after the update was released on Xiao Hei He, it suddenly became a hot topic. Players were all saying, “You have to change it back.” That’s what it means to draw inspiration from the people.
Then there's the coding part. AI Coding: When it comes to developing AI games today, I think the hardest part isn't the game design itself, but rather how to implement something akin to an engine using an engineering-oriented approach.
We developed a set of UGC APIs and created many tools for the AI, enabling it to access in-game weapons such as knives, guns, swords, and so on.For example, a player requested a “hover cannon.” Since the AI has background understanding capabilities, it recognized that a hover cannon is a concept similar to those in Gundam games, while also functioning as a pet. So it combined the game’s pet module with the weapon module to generate the code.
The second topic is gaming five or ten years from now. I believe it will inevitably be closely tied to AI.
First, let’s look at data-driven industries. I’ve observed a reality: the content bubble in content-driven industries is about to burst. Content production costs are skyrocketing, but eventually, the rate at which users consume content will no longer match your production rate, leading to extreme internal competition.
Data-driven industries, meanwhile, may evolve into a hybrid model combining elements of Sora and TikTok—serving as both a content platform and a content distribution channel. Behind the scenes, a series of large language models work together to directly generate content; the content is created by AI, rather than through traditional planning or pre-designed visuals.
What it needs to do is create an editor similar to Roblox’s, while integrating AI capabilities so that the AI can learn, through the collaborative creation process, what kind of content players prefer and how to better create new content. We call this the “Soul of the World,” and it’s the world model we aim to build.
As for the rest, even if they aren’t tied to gameplay, they fall under the production side. When we greenlit *Maggie’s Garden* at the end of 2023, there were roughly 2.9 million Steam accounts. By April 2024, that number had risen to 3.2 million. As of this year, 2025, it has surpassed 4.1 million.
It tripled in less than two years, whereas the user ID before that took over a decade to build up. Could it be that AI is enabling many people who previously lacked the ability to develop Steam games—to go it alone, or for three to five people to form a powerhouse individual or team?
I think the gaming industry will become even more competitive five years from now, because people who originally lacked the ability to work in this industry will become increasingly capable with the help of AI and will have more and more opportunities to express themselves, which may lead to the emergence of a form of mass media.
I started out as a programmer, but now, with the help of the Claude 4.5 model, I don’t need to write a single line of code—I just need to review the final deliverables. The gaming industry will likely look like this in five or ten years.
Tan Liyuan : We’re running a little over time, so I’ll give a brief answer to the second question.
Five to ten years is a long time. My basic assumption is that AI will definitely continue to develop and may even advance beyond general artificial intelligence. First, I believe AI will be integrated quite extensively and deeply into games, and the boundaries won’t be so clear-cut—AI won’t be completely separated into its own distinct category.
When considered on its own, this category is still in a very early stage given the current environment. As experience and technology continue to mature, it should be integrated into games in a relatively natural way, much like high-quality sound effects, art, lighting, and ray tracing.
But looking at it from another angle, since we're talking about a very long time horizon, the way things come together may not be what we currently envision—including the models' ability to understand, their level of understanding, and the cost structure. My view is rather radical; I believe the changes could be quite significant.
Xu Yiran : Okay, thanks. Finally, let’s take a minute to get everyone’s imagination going. I’m sure a lot of you have seen *The Assassination of a Novelist*, right? The other day, after my wife watched it, she said to me, “Aren’t you a game developer? Isn’t this just an AI game?”
"What do you mean?" I asked. She replied, "Look, you can change the virtual world just with words. Once AI becomes powerful enough, won't a whole bunch of people be able to write novels together in the same virtual world, and then that world will change?"
As I mentioned earlier, I believe the integration of channels, content, and data is the trend of the future. In the future, creators and distributors, as well as content producers and consumers, may become one and the same. Everyone will be actively involved in the process, and there may be no distinction between whether you’re a creator or a user.

title: In a popular category crowded with major players, Tencent has finally made its move.
text:
The popular life simulation genre has another standout title. Today, Tencent’s Silver Heart Studio unveiled a new, heartwarming life simulation game set in a miniature world: *Lili’s Miniature World*.
Recently, Tea House was invited to a studio to try out a new game. According to reports, *Lili’s Lilliput* is part of Tencent’s internal “Spring Bamboo Shoot Project,” which aims to explore new areas and incubate unique products. This aligns perfectly with Tea House’s first impression of the game: it’s simply marvelous.
The premise of *Lili’s Lilliput* is quite intriguing. As the title suggests, in this new game, players will shrink in size—much like in *Alice in Wonderland*—and embark on a wondrous journey.But what sets it apart is that *Lili’s Lilliput* revolves around the concept of a “Lilliput right at your fingertips.” With a bedroom desk as the main setting, players will build, explore, garden, and befriend Lili as they embark on a journey of everyday fantasy.
See the world from a smaller perspective; let your imagination take flight, and everyday life becomes “both familiar and unfamiliar.”A forgotten alarm clock can become a rocking chair; a glasses case lined with a blanket turns into a sofa; a wristwatch is repurposed as a clock that holds a few books; and a tape measure can serve as a coffee table… At the hands-on demo, these creations were brought to life in real-world settings.
Real-life scenarios
As everyone wandered around inside, eagerly posing for photos with lollipops in hand, the loneliness and anxiety that come from feeling swallowed up by the vast world seemed to be soothed. It allowed people to rediscover the overlooked beauty in the smallest details and brought to mind the little joys found in watching micro-stop-motion animations like *The Guinea Pig Car*.
On the day of the demo event, the development team also shared the creative vision behind the new game with the media: to build a “Lilliput” right in our own backyard, with “a sense of real life” as the key concept . Starting from the idea of “unique emotional experiences in Lilliput,” they aim to create the simulation game they’ve always envisioned.
To that end, they won’t limit themselves to life simulation genres like Animal Crossing, nor will they label their target audience, nor will they force social interaction… Instead, they’ll incorporate fun life experiences into microgames. Through this approach, they hope to shed light on players’ emotional worlds.
01
Sources of Inspiration
On Life
The creation of *The Little People of Grain* stemmed from an everyday scenario—a dream the team leader had while catching a nap at his desk.
As the team recalls, it was a magical dream in which his body shrank to a tiny size and he found himself back at his desk in real life. Inspired by this magical dream, the team began discussing late into the night during that overtime shift: what kind of wondrous experiences they might have if they shrank down to see the world.That day, everyone’s imaginations ran wild, and they chatted enthusiastically, coming up with many unique ways to explore and experience Lilliput—flying on dandelion seeds and using rulers as musical instruments.
Most importantly, they discovered that when they reopened their eyes to the real world from a smaller perspective, the beauty of life seemed to become even “bigger.”
And so, in the end, this dream became a desk in *Grainland*. Players, now shrunk in size, will build houses on the warm desk, explore all kinds of fantastical worlds, and invite the adorable Grainland creatures to live with them.
02
The Miniature World
Healing Life
This hands-on demo focuses primarily on showcasing the core gameplay features, including dress-up, exploration, building, and spending time with Lili.
First, players can create their own characters. *Grainy’s Lilliput* features a customization system as extensive as that of a dress-up game, with plenty of elements—from accessories and makeup to hairstyles—that players can mix and match as they please.The fashion styles are also diverse—from girls with twin braids to Halloween wizards—allowing players to become trendy and cool kids. What’s more, the overall style of the outfits gives off a warm, fuzzy texture reminiscent of a ball of yarn.
Costume Change Interface and Styles
This plush texture has also found its way into the "Land of Plush" in Lilliput.
In the demo version, the teahouse is the first to appear in a corner of the desk. It’s a unique world with varying elevations. As far as the eye can see—from the streets to the shops—everything has a subjective, fuzzy, textured feel.According to the development team, *Grainy’s Lilliput* revolves around the core concept of “a Lilliput right at your fingertips.” The art style emphasizes a “stylized cartoon rendering” rich in the feel of everyday life—a “Pixar-esque” blend of realistic and picture-book-style whimsy.
And CityWalk in Lilliput also reveals another side of the real world.
The streetscape of Lilliput naturally features green spaces along the roadside, but upon closer inspection, you’ll see that they’re actually cacti wrapped in balls of yarn and dotted with tiny yellow flowers. Walking up to a retail store, you look up and notice that its roof is topped with bottles and jars, with buttons scattered here and there as decorations.Climbing to a higher vantage point, I took a leap into the air, and the teahouse, swaying with its Upah tail, swung back onto the tabletop. I pulled out my skateboard and followed the shifting light and shadows streaming in through the windowsill all the way to the edge. There, suspended in midair, I saw the chair by the table, and my thoughts finally returned to the real world: So, I really am on my desk!
In this demo, the exploration module has also been unlocked. By hailing an Uba car, players can travel to the Morning Dew Flower Field area in the wilderness.
This is a corner of the tea party. As players make their way through the sweet-smelling tulips, they can collect pollen, petals, and dewdrops along the way, and hop on books to gather sunlight. Players can also hop along on the growing centers of little daisies.Sometimes, if you come across a Lucky Puff Daisy or a Wobbly Flower, you can collect large amounts of pollen. These resources will serve as materials for crafting furniture.
Out in the wild, players can also encounter all kinds of Lili. According to team members, the Lili in the game are divided into four basic races. Among them, the Xingyou race most closely resembles humans, while the Bubu race takes the form of small animals; the Yinsuo race consists of robots; and there’s also the Weika race, which is full of eccentrics.Different Lili have different preferences, so you’ll need to arrange their favorite furniture before you can invite them to make their home at your desk.
Different Grains
Overall, the “Lilliput in Our Midst” theme has become a highly distinctive feature within the current life simulation genre, and it has already sparked anticipation for the next gaming experience.
Precisely because of the game’s unique nature, the creative team says, “We face new challenges every day.” Among these, the biggest challenge the team has faced is how to reimagine the world of Lilliput.
“When people are shrunk in size, the density of objects around them increases dramatically, and the team’s workload also increases significantly,” the creative team explained. They noted that this would alter the way the inspiration for Lilliput is brought to life and the logic behind its design, requiring them to meticulously recreate a wealth of details—including the sounds of the wind, rain, and insects that are often overlooked in daily life.
When designing specific scenes, however, they had to balance realism with playability, which often led to many design details being scrapped and redone. Regarding the 3D scene design for the flower field area, the lead designer recalled that the team went through three iterations. They found that focusing solely on 3D pathfinding resulted in a scene that didn’t feel natural to humans.A simple recreation would lack the joy of exploration. In the final version, they needed to ensure that the scene resembled a tea party when viewed from a distance, while still offering engaging gameplay up close.
A Sea of Flowers
They describe it as a process of “having it both ways.” Starting with the desk that has grown alongside players, they hope to create a healing spiritual utopia for them—one that allows people to discover the beauty in their everyday lives through the small objects around them.
03
Back to Everyday Life
Understanding Emotional Support
It’s a bit surprising that Tencent—a company known for its strong social products—has chosen to focus the gaming experience on non-compulsory social interaction this time around.
Not only that, but the three words that Tencent Yinxin’s team repeatedly emphasized during the presentation were “sense of everyday life”— they hope to create a community in *Lili’s Lilliput* that focuses on emotional resonance rather than utilitarian goals, serving as a source of daily companionship.
To blend the gaming experience with the interview content, the “sense of real life” is primarily reflected in aspects such as building, exploration, fashion, and social interaction . However, while these are manifestations of gameplay, the starting point for creating this sense of real life comes from observing everyday life—uncovering the fun in every little detail of daily life and transforming it into gameplay within a miniature world.
Reimagining the functions and ways to play with every everyday object from the perspective of “Lilliput” is a particular test of the team’s imagination. In this regard, the creative team noted that even during the interview process, they look to recruit team members who are passionate about life—and one of the criteria they use to assess this is whether “the interviewee’s eyes light up when talking about their hobbies.”
When people who love life come together, the development process for *Grain’s Lilliput* also breaks down boundaries.Unlike the linear process where designers propose concepts and artists and programmers follow behind to implement them, in this game, everyone can contribute their own ideas. These inspirations are gathered into a “idea pool,” allowing the team to collaboratively bring the microscopic life of Lilliput to life.
And that is precisely why *Grain by Grain: Lilliput* doesn’t just rely on the “Lilliput” theme as a gimmick—it truly allows everyone to experience beautiful moments in their daily lives.
So, in this life simulation and management game, when players find themselves in a sea of flowers, what they collect isn’t wood, stones, or other items—but rather the direct afternoon sunlight and the scent of flowers lingering in the air.From the team’s perspective, these elements embody everyone’s vision of a relaxed atmosphere and the everyday charm of life—and they are precisely the details of daily life that humans, once shrunk in size, might rediscover.
The “Lili Companion” gameplay also incorporates details from everyday life . Team members say they have already designed over 100 Lili residents. Not only do they each have their own preferences and personalities—some are narcissistic, some act like children, and others have a “little adult” personality—but more importantly, they’ll create unique, shared memories with players as they interact.For example, when a player wears a nice outfit, a Lili character might spontaneously compliment them, saying, “That looks great!” Or when a Lili character asks, “Do you prefer sweet or savory mooncakes?” and the player answers that they like sweet ones, they might be delighted to receive a sweet mooncake during the next Mid-Autumn Festival.
The development team stated that their ultimate goal is to create NPCs with distinct personalities, each of whom will respond differently. The game’s character AI module will also be an area they continue to refine.
Previous job postings on the official website
When it comes to clothing, the keyword is “comfort.” In *Lili’s Lilliput*, the clothing is divided into three styles: trendy, special occasions, and the brand’s own line. But no matter what, the team’s standard for comfort is this: “When we see it, we want to wear it ourselves.” At the on-site fashion show, the outfits on display seemed to evoke specific lifestyle scenarios.The White Bear Milk Tea outfit evokes a sense of warmth, while the street graffiti outfit seems like it would let you glide effortlessly through the streets the moment you put it on.
That said, when discussing a new life simulation game these days, what players and the industry are most concerned about is this: Can the game strike a balance between a soothing experience and the grind-and-microtransactions that are almost inevitable in mobile games?
Regarding the monetization model for *Grain by Grain: Lilliput*, the team has not yet provided specific details based on the current progress of the game’s development.However, regarding the game’s grind mechanics, the lead developers have stated that the game as a whole will minimize competition. While players can choose to grind extensively, this process is not driven by a desire to avoid losses; instead, there are many alternative activities (such as cooking and farming) available for players to choose from.
In this regard, the development team also provided the media with additional details about the core gameplay loop of *Li Li's Lilliput*.
Specifically, the game as a whole will revolve around the core gameplay mechanic of “building Lilliput,” which ties together the experiences across different modules.“Players will first explore the world of Lilliput to uncover its backstory and gather various materials needed for daily life. They’ll use these materials to build their own homes and gradually unlock different sections of the desk, allowing them to invite more Lili to their homes and create a wider variety of living scenarios.”
“But there are no time-based requirements,” the development team added. Once the core experience modules have been gradually unlocked, the choice is entirely returned to the players. The development team explained that players can choose to cook and become master chefs, creating recipes for the Land of the Little People.If players want to surround their desk with houseplants, they can spend more time carefully tending to them.
In addition, *Grain of Lilliput* aims to reshape the game’s social mechanics through emotional experiences. The team stated that they will not rely on group-versus-group combat or strategic gameplay as the driving force behind the game’s social interactions; instead, they will recreate real-life social scenarios between strangers within the game.
In the game, they’ll design many touchpoints for players with low or no motivation. It might be a casual chat in a garden during a chance encounter in a public area. It could serve as an icebreaker. Of course, these activities can also be completed solo.The team hopes players will immerse themselves in the experience of exploring Lilliput and slowly build meaningful, close relationships. Once they’ve gotten to know each other, friends can then throw parties together.
Let everything return to its natural state, and let all chance encounters happen naturally. This seems to be the attitude toward life that the team wanted to convey in *Lili’s Lilliput*.
The key to this lies in perception. It’s not just about seeing the positive side, but also recognizing a wider range of emotions. With that in mind, they designed the “Dark Star Well” dungeon, where players can team up with friends to shatter the Dark Star with lollipops. They also noticed stray animals, which inspired them to create Upa.
They also saw themselves reflected in the game. Among the “Grains,” there was a newcomer to the Star’s Edge Association named Dili—who represented the very selves they had once been, when they first decided to set out on a new path.
04
Conclusion
Not limited to category labels
Currently, the life simulation genre is becoming a vertical category that developers are paying close attention to on mobile platforms.
This genre centers on a therapeutic experience. However, when this flow experience is ported to mobile platforms, it is frequently interrupted by the task-based design and forced social interactions typical of mobile games, ultimately turning it into little more than a series of tasks.
Tencent’s Silver Heart team’s *Grain’s Lilliput* is a cross-platform game that introduces the theme of “a Lilliput right at your fingertips,” delivering an innovative take on the genre.The game features building, exploration, and NPC interactions, but how to create an immersive experience centered on a “sense of daily life”—free from the distraction of a quest log—is undoubtedly an aspect the team is still carefully considering and refining.
Regarding the question of “target users” and how they view the “ceiling of the life simulation genre,” the creative team provided a sincere response that also reflected their determination.
They admitted that the life simulation genre is challenging to develop, as the immersive experience it offers places very high demands on the game’s content. However, they also stated that they would focus on themes and emotional experiences to create life simulation games that the team enjoys: “We hope to bring these experiences to life and continually push the boundaries of life simulation.”
They hope that *Lili’s Lilliput* will be a game for all ages that appeals to players who enjoy mixing and matching, collecting, and casual gameplay.He also added, “We didn’t develop this game strictly based on genre conventions; instead, we approached it from the perspective of its theme and the atmosphere it evokes. It’s a kind of ‘pretend play,’ and we hope *Lili’s Lilliput* will offer players a unique Lilliputian experience, just as our slogan says.”
“I’m small, but I live freely.”
Finally, the game’s themed events, user-generated content (UGC), and IP collaborations are all part of its long-term operational plan. Let’s look forward to its next appearance, and following this first reveal, we also look forward to *Grain’s Little World* unveiling more exciting experiences in the future.

title: Chen Xinghan's Unfinished Journey
text:
In the gaming industry, are there still any unexplored blue oceans?
For the 19 years since the company was founded, Chen Xinghan has often used a single image to illustrate what TGC (ThatGameCompany) aims to do.
This chart comes from the British film industry; the x-axis and y-axis represent gender and age, respectively, with film and television genres that cater to different emotional needs plotted on the graph.
The prime real estate in the spectrum is occupied by Disney and Pixar, whose animated films combine the optimistic romance of fantasy, the humor and wit of comedy, and the dramatic twists and turns of drama,and, most importantly, the thought-provoking depth of art house films—capable of bringing tears of joy or sorrow even to adults. These animations are known as “family films for all ages,” capable of moving people of all ages and genders alike.
By creating a map based on human emotional needs and marking the areas covered by games, Chen Xinghan discovered a striking imbalance: most mainstream games are clustered in the upper-left emotional region, much like ships crowding into congested waters.At the center of the map, however, lies a diamond-shaped void—a space that should be filled with emotional experiences enjoyed by people of all ages and genders, much like the territory occupied by Disney and Pixar animations. Chen Xinghan refers to these as “Zone 4 games.”
The gaming industry has been around for decades, with an output value more than double that of the film industry, yet it has yet to produce a true “family-friendly” title.Nintendo once came close to tapping into this untapped market—based on motion controls and the concept of family entertainment, the Wii console launched in 2006 attracted many people who had never played video games before, ultimately selling more than 100 million units, with the accompanying game *Wii Sports* selling 80 million copies,nearly realizing then-President Satoru Iwata’s vision of “expanding the gaming population.”
However, due to a lack of fresh content, the Wii’s glory days did not last. Since then, we’ve rarely seen heartwarming scenes of families sitting on the couch playing games together; instead, people have been talking more about how mobile games are driving them apart.
Some have attempted to analyze the Wii’s “failure” and drawn the lesson that abandoning core gamers and embracing casual users is a risky move. Chen Xinghan doesn’t see it that way; for the past 19 years, he has been striving to introduce new emotional dimensions into games, with the goal of helping more people fall in love with gaming.
“If adults don’t feel moved by it, they’ll think this movie is just for kids—a Saturday morning cartoon, not a Pixar film.” This is also one of the reasons Chen Xinghan believes the Wii’s success failed to last.
He wants to use a product to change the public's perception of games and, in turn, shift the mindset of game developers.
Just as animation was once considered entertainment for children before the advent of Disney and Pixar, the release of *Frozen* and *Toy Story* changed that perception. When adults, too, began to be emotionally moved by these films, people started to recognize the artistic value of this medium.More importantly, after Pixar’s *Toy Story* grossed over $100 million, Sony also established a CG animation studio, followed by DreamWorks and Blue Sky Studios—each employing thousands of staff members.
Just as Disney and Pixar have done—by opening up new markets and proving that games that touch people’s hearts can also achieve commercial success and attract more people to join the journey—this is the goal Chen Xinghan hopes *Sky: Children of the Light* will achieve: to use market forces to validate the existence of demand and drive greater supply.
Six years after its launch, *Sky: Children of the Light* has partially achieved this goal—the game’s commercial performance has far exceeded even the most optimistic initial expectations. Yet, despite this clear success story, very few peers have followed in its footsteps.
At the same time, the gaming industry today is facing a paradox: while industry professionals feel lost because their past experiences are no longer relevant, they continue to turn a blind eye to the new opportunities Chen Xinghan has uncovered.
01
Another Dimension of Human Nature
In its sixth year since launch, *Sky: Children of the Light* has reached a new high in daily active users.
This goes somewhat against the typical patterns of a game's lifecycle—most blockbuster games begin to decline two or three years after launch and then enter a prolonged period of decline.
At this stage, the industry as a whole is grappling with a certain dilemma: aside from a handful of evergreen games, many titles are rapidly declining in popularity. Yet when launching new projects, developers are unsure what new markets or genres to pursue, leaving them with no choice but to compete over IPs and art design.
In the pursuit of high-quality games, some leading projects have teams numbering in the hundreds or even thousands, essentially turning game development into a matter of human resource management. Meanwhile, TGC has fewer than 300 employees company-wide, with R&D staff making up less than half of that total, yet its metrics continue to grow against the trend. Why is that?
Unlike game companies that simply chase commercial success, TGC has had an unusual goal since its inception: to infuse games with more positive emotions, to move even those who don’t normally play games, and to make games an art form recognized by society at large, just like novels and movies.
Nineteen years have passed, and the industry has seen its ups and downs, with mainstream players shifting from PCs and consoles to more convenient mobile devices, but Chen Xinghan’s goal has never changed.
As the company’s most commercially successful product, *Sky: Children of the Light* underwent seven years of development and six years of continuous operation; Chen Xinghan devoted 13 years of his life to this game—nearly one-third of his life.
Today, *Sky: Children of the Light* has earned many accolades that are the envy of its peers: long-term operation, high DAU, multiplayer social interaction, UGC… These terms all point to the key to the game’s enduring success. But in Chen Xinghan’s eyes, *Sky: Children of the Light* is a “platform of goodwill” that helps people forge genuine emotional connections.
In psychology, there is a term called “nudge,” which refers to “influencing people’s decisions through subtle interventions to guide them toward certain choices.” This is very common in game design.
In a sense, game designers are like lawmakers; by altering the laws and natural laws of the virtual world, they can “nudge” people’s behavioral tendencies toward the vulgar or the noble.
When designers hold the power to set rules and guide interactions, different values can lead to vastly different outcomes.Games driven solely by commercial goals often exploit human weaknesses: using virtual currency to obscure real-world prices, employing random rewards to induce gambling addiction, and stoking mutual hatred to drive spending on warfare. But Chen Xinghan believes that “legislators” should uphold ethical standards.
In *Sky: Children of the Light*, there are no levels, no combat, and no leaderboards.To foster a friendlier environment for player interaction and make the game more welcoming to introverts, *Sky: Children of the Light* has set certain requirements for in-game socializing: players must first unlock actions like holding hands, high-fives, and hugs before they can start chatting. When opportunities to connect are hard to come by, people tend to cherish them all the more.
It is the many subtle details that collectively make *Sky: Children of the Light* unique, and each unconventional design choice required time to conceive, refine, and test—which is why the game took a full seven years to develop before its release.
As a game in continuous operation, the official launch is just the beginning of a long journey. As large numbers of players join the game, the diverse feedback they provide serves as the basis for designers to improve the game, introducing elements of “co-creation” into this virtual society.
“*Sky: Children of the Light* has over 20 million monthly active users—that’s equivalent to four Norways or one Shanghai.” With so many people, there are bound to be different opinions and feedback; I really feel like we’re drafting laws and revising policies.”Chen Xinghan said that beyond “legislating,” the *Sky: Children of the Light* team must also maintain order and foster a positive atmosphere within the community, shouldering responsibilities akin to “governing.”
It’s inevitable that a leader’s inbox will be flooded with complaints from citizens. Chen Xinghan has publicly shared touching letters from players, but he rarely mentions that he now wakes up every day to find dozens of complaint emails in his inbox—there are always those in favor and those against.
He showed me a player’s handwritten notebook containing 35 suggestions for improving *Sky: Children of the Light*, along with a box full of similar feedback. He carries these with him and flips through them from time to time.
“I visited three cities last year, and in each city, about 300 people wrote down their opinions.” From last year’s in-person events alone, Chen Xinghan collected 900 pieces of feedback. “I tallied them up to see what came up most frequently—and what were the second and third most common issues—and then shared the results with my team.”
It's a huge amount of work, and players' opinions often conflict with one another. Sometimes he even finds himself wondering, "What kind of job is this?"
“But if you don’t take the time to listen, you’ll end up making the wrong decision, and more people will be disappointed.” He acknowledged that designers often underestimate the complexity of human nature and inevitably mean well but end up doing more harm than good; however, it’s only after experiencing many such situations that one can learn to truly listen by learning from one’s mistakes.
When I talk with Chen Xinghan, I often get the impression that he approaches things from a different perspective on human nature. The “reverse growth” in *Sky: Children of the Light* stems from every aspect of how he does things and is closely tied to his values.
02
A Different Starting Point
As a teenager, Chen Xinghan once shed tears while playing *The Legend of Sword and Fairy* and *Final Fantasy*. Games allowed him to experience the feeling of “loss,” prompting him to reflect on how to avoid such loss, how to live his life, and how to become a better person.
An idea began to take root: if a creator can use their work to improve the lives of their audience, then he must do the same. Although at the time, he didn’t yet know that games would become his medium of expression.
It all really began in 2006 with Chen Xinghan’s senior thesis project at the University of Southern California—*Clouds*. At first, he wanted to create a game similar to *SimCity*, but his advisor, Tracy Fullerton, asked, “Does your game have a protagonist?”
“What kind of protagonist does *SimCity* need?” Chen Xinghan asked, puzzled.
“What if the main character were a child?”
To fulfill his advisor’s requirements, Chen Xinghan began thinking about how to introduce a protagonist into the game. He delved into his memories: as an only child who suffered from asthma, he had spent much of his childhood in solitude.While his classmates were running around the playground during P.E. class, he could only lie in bed or sit alone in an empty classroom. Gazing out the window at Shanghai’s gray, hazy sky, he fantasized about flying up to the clouds, gathering the dark clouds to bring down a refreshing rain that would wash away the city’s pollution.
“Subconsciously, I felt the city needed a good wash.” In his memory, after it rained, he could smell the freshness of the earth and the scent of grass, and the city seemed even more beautiful.
And so, *Cloud* was born—a little boy flies up into the sky, plays with the clouds, and purifies the world with rain. This small game, created by a group of students from scratch without the use of any game engine, unexpectedly touched the hearts of many people.
Prior to this, Chen Xinghan had created more than one game, but they were all student projects based on existing games. *Cloud* was the first time he incorporated his own experiences and emotions into a game, and it was also the first time he received letters from players.
Strangers from all over the country wrote letters thanking *Cloud* for the wonderful experience it provided,some saying it was the first time a game had moved them to tears. In their letters, they encouraged Chen Xinghan to start a company and create more games that touch people’s hearts, showing society that games aren’t just about competition and killing—they can also be rich in emotion and make people’s lives better. This is precisely the true reason behind the founding of TGC.
Some people have written in to say that, although they had never played video games before, they were deeply captivated by *Cloud*. This made Chen Xinghan particularly happy—he had finally sparked an interest in video games among people who didn’t play them, fulfilling his childhood dream.
However, *Cloud* also revealed some issues: the game is “too difficult,” and while it attracted a group of players, many of them eventually gave up because they couldn’t get the hang of the keyboard and mouse controls. This left Chen Xinghan feeling regretful: “I finally managed to get this group interested, only for their final experience to be so terrible.”
He realized that when faced with entirely new needs and audiences, even the most obvious assumptions could fail—you might think “WASD” (keyboard controls) is simple, but to someone who doesn’t play games, it’s a foreign language. To enable people who don’t know how to play games to enjoy them, he needed to build from the ground up.
Since there were no established models to draw upon in the gaming industry, he turned to older disciplines and found inspiration in positive psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi’s “flow theory”: when challenges and abilities are in balance, people enter a state of complete absorption. Since players have different skill levels at different stages of the game, the appropriate level of challenge should also vary accordingly.
Based on this theory, Chen Xinghan proposed the “Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment” (DDA) design method and created *Flow* to test his hypothesis—a game that appears extremely simple, in which players control microorganisms as they swim, feed, and evolve in the primordial ocean, adjusting the difficulty through their own choices.
This little game, created by a tech guy to test his mental model, unexpectedly racked up 6 million downloads, allowing players of all skill levels to enjoy it. Later, the game also served as the stepping stone that led to TGC signing a deal with Sony.
*Cloud* and *Flow*, two games created during his student years, served as the catalysts for Chen Xinghan to found TGC and collaborate with Sony, respectively. They also established TGC’s approach in its early stages: to explore new emotional dimensions in games and to engage a broader audience through innovative design.
03
Awe and Vulnerability
“Our core focus is on meeting the emotional needs shared by everyone, and then building games from scratch,” Chen Xinghan told me.
Having no reference points is perhaps the most daunting challenge for game developers. But Chen Xinghan chose a completely different path. In his view, following in the footsteps of those who came before would result in a lot of unnecessary bloat; only by starting from the very basics can one create a design that perfectly suits the target audience.
When TGC was developing its third game, *Flower*, the team attempted to completely abandon traditional control schemes, retaining only a single button and relying on a six-axis sensor to determine movement direction. Players tilt the controller to control the wind and guide the petals as they dance through the air. The design is so simple that even players with disabilities can enjoy the game.
The game eventually made its way into the Smithsonian American Art Museum, where it was recognized as a work of art. However, during development, the team faced significant challenges because there were no precedents to draw upon. The game took two years to develop, with 14 of those months spent hitting a wall.
However, this has not altered Chen Xinghan and TGC’s product philosophy; they continue to introduce new emotions and explore new designs in their latest works.
After *Flower*, TGC spent three years developing *Journey*, including a year and a half of trial and error; the subsequent success of this indie game finally established them as a major player in the industry.
"Journey" was inspired by Chen Xinghan's feelings of loneliness while pursuing his graduate studies in the United States. At the time, he had just arrived in the country, struggled with English, and had to work five jobs to make ends meet, all while harboring a deep-seated longing to connect with others.
How can we overcome loneliness? Chen Xinghan painted a picture: a giant walking on a snow-capped mountain, while people at the foot of the mountain walk hand in hand—one false step and they’ll be trampled to death. Visibility is extremely low in the thick fog, so people can only rely on the guidance of those ahead of them to ensure their safety.
“Someone is holding my hand, completely dependent on me to survive, and I, in turn, depend on the person ahead of me.” Chen Xinghan believes that this kind of interdependence may be the only way for people to escape loneliness. He wants to capture this feeling through his games, allowing players to truly feel, in a single moment, that they are not alone.
Most games on the market encourage players to compete—so how can we make people interdependent in games? TGC spent a long time mulling over this question until Chen Xinghan found inspiration during a conversation with an astronaut.
Chen Xinghan noticed a mysterious phenomenon: after returning to Earth, astronauts who had landed on the moon all began to seek faith and became exceptionally devout—even if they had originally been die-hard scientists.
Curiosity drove him to track down the first astronaut to drive a lunar rover.When asked what was on the moon, the man’s answer was unexpected: the moon was the most boring place he had ever been—no color, just dust. In this silent, colorless world, the only interesting thing in the universe was Earth, and you could cover it with just your thumb.
“Once you’ve left Earth behind, you find yourself in the most vast expanse in the world. You begin to wonder: Why am I here? Why are we on that tiny planet? What is the meaning of the entire universe? You’re suddenly overwhelmed by a feeling—the realization that you’re just a speck of dust in the universe.”
That feeling is awe—an emotion that is becoming increasingly rare in modern life.
“We live in a world of empowerment,” Chen Xinghan observed. “We can travel at 80 miles per hour, talk to people in any corner of the world, and get answers to any question in a matter of milliseconds. When was the last time we felt small?”
This tendency toward empowerment is particularly evident in the gaming industry. Virtually all mainstream games cater to players’ fantasies of power—playing the hero, conquering the world, and being invincible. When players feel powerful, their first instinct is often to exert that power over others. Even in cooperative games, the focus remains on enhancing individual abilities.
Under the logic of traditional online games, players are given the ability to kill and plunder, so naturally they do not value their connections with others. Chen Xinghan realized that to help players form genuine emotional bonds, this power dynamic must be reversed.
In contrast to strength is vulnerability, which is precisely the key to triggering empathy.
From an evolutionary perspective, this is a survival instinct of social animals. Weak individuals must rely on one another to survive; it is precisely the fear of risk and a sense of insignificance that foster these bonds.Chen Xinghan believes that these two emotions—awe and vulnerability—define the essence of human connection: our vulnerability when we are alone drives our longing for a sense of belonging.
Based on these considerations, *Journey* adopted an unconventional design: players have no weapons and can only evade threats or rely on their companions; the environment is powerful and dangerous, with the desert’s scorching sun and the icy winds of the snow-capped mountains constantly draining their energy; there is no gear to collect or experience points to earn—simply being with one’s companions is the greatest reward.
The environment shapes human behavior, and by creating a world that evokes a sense of awe and vulnerability, *Journey* successfully fosters empathy among players. Ultimately, the game conveys the feeling that people walk alone through the vast desert, only to chance upon a kindred spirit with whom they can journey through life.
After the release of *Journey*, TGC received over 1,600 thank-you letters from players; the game moved many to tears. It also won more than 180 awards, broke two Guinness World Records, and was included in the collections of several museums, catapulting Chen Xinghan and TGC to prominence in the industry.
04
The Scent of a Pirate
"Journey" not only moved players but also inspired many people in the gaming industry, including two Chinese students studying game design at New York University—Chen Ji and Zhang Zhechuan.
In 2013, they began preparing their final project, *Twins*. Unlike the assigned projects they had worked on during their studies, this time they wanted to create a unique emotional experience. Through the department chair, they got in touch with Chen Xinghan and received his guidance.
"Twins" took over three years to develop. In the game, players control a small star and, together with their companions, soar through the sky, overcoming obstacles to illuminate the world.After graduation, Chen Ji joined TGC as a designer on *Sky: Children of the Light*, while Zhang Zhechuan returned to China to join Tencent NExT Studios, where he created the critically acclaimed *Sound of a Murder Case*.
Zhang Zhechuan recalled to me that one incident from back then left a deep impression on him: Chen Xinghan told him that while *Journey* had received excellent reviews, it wasn’t particularly successful commercially and couldn’t prove to game developers who wanted to create similar works that this was a viable path forward.His next goal was to create a profitable game that would prove this genre’s commercial viability—rather than being merely idealistic—and that game became *Sky: Children of the Light*.
“Now that *Sky: Children of the Light* has proven itself to be a profitable game, why aren’t there still more projects like it?” I asked.
“The success of *Sky: Children of the Light* is inseparable from Mr. Chen’s years of experience, yet it is not the kind of success that could have been predicted from a traditional commercial project planning perspective.” In Zhang Zhechuan’s view, this runs counter to the logic of major studios, which typically require mature benchmarks and predictable data before greenlighting a project.
Without any models to reference, it meant reinventing the wheel from scratch. *Sky: Children of the Light* took seven years to develop—a development cycle long enough to deter most commercial companies.More importantly, as a game designed for long-term operation, *Sky: Children of the Light* incorporates multiplayer online elements, social features, user-generated content (UGC), and innovative business models. These design elements are tightly intertwined and may only work effectively in *Sky: Children of the Light*; others would be hesitant to imitate them—and even if they tried, they likely couldn’t replicate them.
“Teacher Chen and his team built the emotional experience from scratch and then developed the business model from scratch as well—it’s extremely risky, and most companies wouldn’t do it that way,” Zhang Zhechuan told me. Validating a business model is very difficult, and the cost of trial and error is extremely high. The approach taken by the vast majority of companies is this: once a few games succeed and validate a set of monetization strategies, they simply keep replicating that model.
Many companies don’t even build user experiences from scratch; they merely engage in incremental innovation. The pursuit of certainty means that most companies need to identify clear benchmarks when launching projects and rely on proven designs for their implementation strategies.
“When project approval becomes driven by short-term gains, design becomes driven by short-term gains as well, and under such circumstances, it’s difficult to create games like *Light·Encounter* and *Journey*,” said Zhang Zhechuan.
Chen Xinghan and TGC’s development model is highly idealistic—it starts with emotional needs and builds the experience from the ground up to avoid the redundancy caused by inappropriate experiences. This requires the team to have exceptional design capabilities, ample time, and room for exploration.However, traditional commercial companies rarely provide such an environment or the patience required; independent teams, on the other hand, are more likely to persist with this kind of exploration. This is also one of the reasons Zhang Zhechuan left a major tech company to start his own business.
Compared to mainstream commercial games, Chen Xinghan has a greater appreciation for indie games. Every year at GDC (Game Developers Conference), he almost always visits the indie game exhibition area, where young people with diverse ideas gather, full of energy—he actually met TGC’s first programmer there. In his view, it is in places like this that one can see the future of gaming.
Chen Xinghan believes there is a paradox in the industry: “You can’t put profitability first and innovation second. Because prioritizing profitability will force you to gravitate toward proven business models.”
“What is an indie game? It’s making games that you really want to create, even though their commercial viability hasn’t been proven yet. It’s full of risks, but developers can visualize that game in their minds and aren’t willing to give up on pursuing it.” Chen Xinghan said, “That’s the spirit of a pirate—believing that treasure lies in places not yet charted on the map. If you’re just in it for the money, you’re better off joining a big studio and becoming part of the navy.”
Chen Xinghan knows the owner of a game company who has made billions of dollars. This person often expresses envy toward those who create unique games, but says he plans to make some money first and then innovate once he’s made enough.
“I asked him, ‘How much do you need to make before you’re satisfied?’ He said, ‘It’s still not enough—I want to make a little more,’” Chen Xinghan said. “I think he’ll probably never really make a game that stands out from the rest in his entire life.”
05
A Company for Everyone
“The production team is now operating on autopilot,” Chen Xinghan said. “I don’t have to micromanage it—it runs smoothly on its own.”
Compared to his early years, one of the biggest changes for Chen Xinghan is that he has learned to let go. Back then, he had to handle many things himself, but now many of the up-and-coming designers are capable of taking on responsibilities on their own.
TGC has been developing games for 19 years, with five titles to its credit, and the core members of its development team have been working together for over a decade. Compared to many top-tier projects with ever-expanding teams, TGC’s team is relatively small. In Chen Xinghan’s view, bigger isn’t necessarily better when it comes to teams. He compares game development to filmmaking—while a movie may involve hundreds of people, the core crew consists of only about 10 people.
“Hiring more people who score 70 doesn’t increase talent density—it actually dilutes it. Reducing the number of 70s and 80s and keeping only the 90s—the headcount may shrink, but the concentration increases.” Today, TGC has over 200 employees; while communication costs have risen slightly, the company is still running smoothly.
Unlike the pyramid-shaped structure found in most game companies—where the producer is at the top, followed by the lead designer, lead artist, lead programmer, and so on—the organizational structure of the *Sky: Children of the Light* development team is more decentralized: designers take the lead in generating ideas, and anyone can propose concepts for new seasons.
Their way of thinking is quite unlike that of a typical “game company”—they don’t design features just to boost metrics. Take the fishing system, for example: they didn’t consider creating a collection guide where players would have to catch 80 different types of fish just to extend their playtime. Instead, they focused on questions like: Where should the caught fish go? Does this fit with the world of *Sky: Children of the Light*? Because *Sky: Children of the Light* is a real world.
Most TGC employees have a “second talent”—some are passionate about movies, some are knowledgeable about music, and some are audio enthusiasts… In a team like this, with so many voices speaking up, disagreements and lost efficiency are inevitable, but Chen Xinghan wants the company to be exactly like this.
He admires Pixar's culture and even brought in Pixar founder Ed Catmull as a consultant.
Pixar used to have a beautiful long table that could seat 30 people facing each other in two rows. The director and producer sat in the middle, with everyone else seated on either side. To help everyone find their seats, the secretary would print out place cards.
This table had been in use for more than a decade. It wasn’t until a meeting at a square table in a small conference room—where he noticed everyone sitting in relaxed postures and communicating freely—that Katem suddenly realized: this was exactly the kind of interaction he wanted.Although management had always emphasized that rank didn’t matter, the seating arrangement at the long table sent the opposite message—that the opinions of those seated in the middle were important, while those on the edges were not. Immediately after the meeting, he got rid of the long table and removed the place cards.
Pixar’s “think tank” system also embodies the principle of equality. The think tank is composed of key employees from various positions and levels, who regularly provide feedback on film rough cuts. Even the company’s cooks and cleaning staff write reviews of new films, which directors are required to read carefully.
Interestingly, Steve Jobs, as the boss, never participated—this was an agreement between him and Catmull, because Catmull knew full well that Jobs’s strong personality would intimidate people into not speaking honestly, thereby undermining the atmosphere of candor.To encourage young people to speak up, they also had an unwritten rule: for the first 15 minutes of every meeting, veteran director John Lasseter had to remain silent.
Their goal is to ensure that the creative process is driven by the best ideas, rather than by hierarchical rank.
Chen Xinghan agrees with this philosophy. In an atmosphere of equality and openness, the company has shifted from being dominated by the will of a few to a place where everyone creates for themselves.
06
An Unfinished Journey
Six years after its launch, *Sky: Children of the Light* has far exceeded Chen Xinghan’s most optimistic commercial expectations at the time, but there are still some regrets.
Let’s return to the chart mentioned earlier. *Sky: Children of the Light* has only achieved three-quarters of the “Four-Zone Game” goal: while it has won the hearts of mothers and daughters, it hasn’t managed to spark much interest among sons.
Involving young boys as well to create a truly family-friendly experience—that is the goal Chen Xinghan plans to achieve with his next game.
“Just like Pixar and Disney animated films,” he said, “If other media have a market like this, why can’t video games?”
